title: The Miller of Sanssouci
text:
In the 1740s Frederick the Great of Prussia built his summer palace, Sanssouci, on a hill at Potsdam. Close to it stood a windmill, which still stands there today in rebuilt form.

According to a famous story, the king was annoyed by the mill, its noise or the way it spoiled his view, and offered to buy it so it could be torn down. The miller refused to sell the mill his family had worked. The king lost patience and reminded the miller that he could simply take it without paying. The miller answered that he could, if there were no judges in Berlin. In the story, the king was pleased by this faith in Prussian justice and let the mill stand.

The tale spread across Europe, especially after the French writer Andrieux turned it into a verse tale in 1797, and the miller's reply became a proverb for the rule of law.

There is an irony behind it. In the real case of a miller named Arnold in 1779, Frederick overruled the courts, believing they had wronged a poor miller, and had the judges arrested and imprisoned.
lesson: Power is most trustworthy when it accepts the same rules as everyone else. A leader who respects limits on himself earns lasting authority.
source: Prussian popular tradition; Francois Andrieux, Le Meunier de Sans-Souci (1797)
caveat: There is no reliable evidence that the conversation took place; it is a legend that grew around a real mill.
